title: OpenClaw in Your Hand: Building a Physical AI Terminal - Lech Kalinowski, Callstack

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk describes a physical AI terminal that serves as a harness for OpenClaw agents and local LLMs, with a firmware-to-backend control plane dispatching to models, agents, and a game engine. The device is a general-purpose AI terminal with no specific industry vertical, framed as a 'Game Boy for LLMs.' The project is a 3-month prototype with 130 commits, ongoing engineering failures, and a provisional patent filing. The content spans embedded systems hardware engineering, LLM serving infrastructure, and LLM-native game design. This is a conference presentation with recorded device demonstrations. Classification is supported by multiple direct transcript excerpts spanning device motivation, firmware architecture, backend inference, and product framing.

summary: Lech Kalinowski frames his talk with a fictional story of discovering a strange shell-powered device in his basement, then reveals the real motivation: building a physical, AI-native device that feels calm rather than distracting. The device, called Vault, is a text-first handheld terminal built on an ESP32-S3 dual-core microcontroller powered by a single lithium polymer cell. Its defining design choice is a dual-display approach: a small monochrome OLED serves as a fast, emissive live surface for typing and dynamic content, while a bistable e-paper display serves as a slow content surface for rendered output. This combination addresses e-paper's slowness for dynamic text while preserving energy efficiency and readability. The firmware renders using fixed static buffers with one-bit images stored in pre-allocated memory—no markdown engine and no malloc on the MCU side. Four modes are accessible via a single slash command: an internal shell for system settings and Wi-Fi, an assist mode for LLM interaction, a control mode for OpenClaw agents, and an LLM-native RPG mode. The backend architecture keeps all inference server-side: a dependency-free Python backend handles agentic work via OpenClaw, serves a 120-billion-parameter open-source GPT model using NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM, and exposes an OpenAI-style API proxy because not all open-source models conform to the OpenAI API specification. Engineering field notes document several day-costing failures: software I2C required proper control without physical pull-ups, GPIO 13 had silent failures necessitating a port change, a power supply regulator destroyed LEDs and fragile display parts with replacement parts taking weeks, and a cheap encoder introduced rotational noise requiring additional pull-ups and capacitors. Two displays were blown up during prototyping. The RPG mode is a standout feature: Kalinowski built four worlds (cyberpunk, fantasy/Witcher-inspired, deep-space void, and another), with LLM-generated characters, maps, skills, and personalities, all converted to one-bit matrices for display. The device is designed to be bulletproof—failures in one component leave fallbacks. Kalinowski filed a provisional patent targeting a niche market for quiet, distraction-free AI devices without audio or video interfaces. He closes with a recorded demo showing boot, Wi-Fi connection, help command, OpenClaw agent checking DGX Spark disk space, and RPG world selection. In his final remarks, he highlights the paradox that a quiet text-interface game requires the most powerful GPU in the world, and reframes the entire project as a 'Game Boy'—a device to play with LLMs—while thanking Callstack's technological incubator for their support.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Framing Story
sections.summary: Kalinowski opens with a fictional story of finding a dusty, shell-powered device from the 1980s in his basement that responds in natural language. He then reveals the real motivation: building a physical, AI-native device that feels like it comes from the future, starting as a remote controller for his OpenClaw instance on a DGX Spark.

sections.title: Device Design: Dual-Display Architecture and Four Modes
sections.summary: Explains the dual-display approach: a small monochrome OLED for fast dynamic text input (live surface) paired with a bistable e-paper for rendered content. The ESP32 dual-core MCU runs firmware with four modes—shell, assist, control, and RPG—accessible via a single slash command. Rendering uses fixed static buffers with one-bit images in pre-allocated memory, with no markdown engine or malloc on the MCU.

sections.title: Backend Architecture and Model Serving
sections.summary: Describes the full backend architecture: Vault firmware on the terminal communicates with a dependency-free Python backend handling OpenClaw agentic work and LLM serving. The local model is a 120-billion-parameter open-source GPT served via NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM, with an OpenAI-style API proxy because not all open-source models match the OpenAI API specification. Shows an example of OpenClaw writing and storing Java code locally.

sections.title: Engineering Field Notes and Lessons Learned
sections.summary: Shares day-costing engineering failures: software I2C needed proper control without physical pull-ups, GPIO 13 had silent failures requiring a port change, a power supply regulator destroyed LEDs and fragile display parts with replacement parts taking weeks, and a cheap encoder introduced rotational noise requiring additional pull-ups and capacitors. Two displays were blown up during prototyping.

sections.title: RPG Mode and LLM-Native Game Design
sections.summary: Details the LLM-native RPG mode, inspired by text-based role-playing games Kalinowski never got to play. Four worlds were created: cyberpunk, Witcher-inspired fantasy, deep-space void, and another. The LLM generates characters, worlds, maps, skills, and personalities, all converted to one-bit matrices for display. The device is described as bulletproof with fallbacks for component failures.

sections.title: IP, Market Niche, and Project Numbers
sections.summary: Discusses filing a provisional patent for quiet, distraction-free AI devices—a niche most manufacturers ignore by focusing on audio and video. Shares project stats: 130 commits over 3 months, 4 modes, 4 RPG worlds, 16 classes, tiny fast firmware, single lithium polymer cell. Takeaways: keep models on the backend (too heavy for MCUs), and narrative context matters more than numbers.

sections.title: Recorded Demo Walkthrough
sections.summary: Shows a recorded demo: device boot, Wi-Fi connection, welcome and main screens, help command, tutorials, OpenClaw agent checking DGX Spark disk space, and RPG mode with four worlds (Older guns, Neon abyss, The hollows, Void witch), character selection, and LLM-generated content. Notes the irony that a text game without 3D graphics uses the most advanced NVIDIA processor in the DGX Spark.

sections.title: Closing Remarks and Acknowledgments
sections.summary: Kalinowski closes by reiterating the paradox that a quiet text-interface game requires the most powerful GPU in the world. He reframes the entire presentation: while it covered a handheld device to control OpenClaw agents with local LLMs, in general it was about building a 'Game Boy'—a device to play with LLMs. He thanks Callstack for their support through their technological incubator, which made the work possible.
